stances.claim: The 1946 Treaty of General Relations is the 'mother' of PH-US defense relations -- through it the US relinquished sovereignty over the Philippines except in existing military bases, and from it descend three foundational defense pacts (1947 MBA, 1947 MAA, 1951 MDT) that together define the legal architecture of the alliance.

The Sept 16, 1991 Senate 'Magnificent Twelve' rejection of the bases-extension treaty 'satisfied Filipino nationalists but minimized America's ability to project its power in the Western Pacific' -- and the resulting power vacuum gave China the opportunity to replace America as the dominant regional power; this is the structural origin of the present SCS dispute.

The alliance has been progressively rebuilt since 1991 through a layered sequence -- VFA (May 27, 1999, upheld in Bayan v Zamora), post-9/11 Balikatan (Jan 2002) for al-Qaida-linked Mindanao insurgency, 2002 MLSA, and the 2014 Edca (8 rounds of negotiations) -- reflecting both PH need and US 'pivot to Asia' coinciding with the 2013 PH arbitration filing after Scarborough.

The Edca expands US access to PH bases on a rotational basis and authorizes new facility construction, prepositioning of defense equipment, and access to 'agreed locations' -- operationally the most significant deepening since the 1991 bases ouster, justifying CJ Sereno's Saguisag opinion that upheld its constitutionality.

notable_anecdotes: The 'mother' treaty framing: 'This treaty became the mother of our defense relationship with the United States. Pursuant thereto, three defense pacts were concluded' -- using genealogy metaphor to organize the legal architecture.

The 'Magnificent Twelve' Senate rejection -- preserved as the operative historical pivot moment, with the immediate consequences ('satisfied Filipino nationalists') balanced against the strategic cost ('minimized America's ability to project its power... The power vacuum gave China the opportunity to replace America').
The MBA's original 99-year/2046 horizon vs the negotiated reduction to 44 years/1991 -- using the dramatic timeline compression to physicalize PH negotiating leverage gains over decades.

9/11 as relationship pivot: 'After the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center in New York City on Sept. 11, 2001, PH-US defense relations entered a new phase' -- using a single date to mark structural transition in the alliance.
Balikatan's specific origin: January 2002 US arrivals in Mindanao 'to take part in the Balikatan, simulating joint military maneuvers in case of an armed attack' against al-Qaida-linked insurgency.

The serial-column teaser closing: 'will our defense pacts with the United States help or hinder us in addressing our concerns in the South China Sea? This question deserves an answer next Sunday. Abangan.' -- using Tagalog 'Abangan' (watch out for it) as the column's signature serial-tease device.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reviews PH-US defense relations amid increasing regional tension from US-China SCS military exercises (Russia joining in September) and US Secretary of State John Kerry's recent visit. The relationship was highlighted in CJ Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno's Saguisag v Ochoa decision (Jan 12, 2016) upholding the Edca's constitutionality. After the 1898 Battle of Manila Bay and the Treaty of Paris (Spain ceded PH to US), the July 4, 1946 'independence' was concurrent with the 1946 Treaty of General Relations -- the 'mother' of PH-US defense relations -- through which the US relinquished sovereignty over the Philippines except in existing military bases. From it descended three defense pacts: the 1947 Military Bases Agreement (MBA, 23 bases, 99 years/2046, subsequently amended to 44 years/1991 with returned bases, recognized PH sovereignty over Clark and Subic, mandatory 5-year reviews, and prior-consultation requirements); the 1947 Military Assistance Agreement (MAA, an executive agreement covering arms, ammunition, supplies, equipment, vessels, services, and training); and the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT, Aug 30, 1951) with two features -- mutual assistance in maintaining individual and collective defense capacities, and mutual self-defense against armed attack on either party's territory. On Sept 16, 1991, the Senate's 'Magnificent Twelve' rejected the proposed bases-extension treaty, satisfying Filipino nationalists but minimizing America's Western Pacific power projection -- the resulting vacuum 'gave China the opportunity to replace America as the dominant power in our region.' Joint military exercises continued in the 1990s; large-scale drills were suspended in 1995 and later resumed at reduced level. The alliance was formally revived via the 1999 Visiting Forces Agreement (upheld in Bayan v Zamora, Oct 10, 2000), with VFA II as the counterpart for PH personnel in the US. After the Sept 11, 2001 World Trade Center attacks, US forces arrived in Mindanao in January 2002 for Balikatan exercises combating al-Qaida-linked insurgency, and the 2002 Mutual Logistics Support Agreement (extended twice, expiring 2017) regulated reciprocal logistics. In 2013, the PH filed arbitration after China's Scarborough Shoal occupation -- coinciding with Obama's 'pivot to Asia' -- and after eight rounds of negotiations the two countries signed Edca, expanding rotational US base access, authorizing new facility construction, prepositioning defense equipment, and granting access to 'agreed locations.' CJ closes with a serial-tease: will our defense pacts with the US help or hinder us in addressing our SCS concerns? 'Abangan.'
